name: Benin Empire

fields.foundation: The Benin Empire grew out of a gradual process of political centralisation in the forest lowlands of what is now southern Nigeria. It began in the ancient Edo settlement of Igodomigodo, later Benin City, which tradition holds was ruled by the Ogiso (“kings of the sky”) dynasty for several centuries before the establishment of the Oba dynasty around 1180 CE. The transition is associated with Eweka I, a figure partly of legend, who was installed as the first Oba after a period of crisis in which the Ogiso line had lost legitimacy. The early Obas steadily built up royal authority against the uzama, the hereditary chiefs who had acted as kingmakers and a check on royal power. Oba Ewedo (13th century) moved the palace to its permanent site, renamed the state Edo and created palace offices that shifted power from hereditary chiefs towards royal appointees. His successor Oguola is credited with the first phase of the great earthwork walls and moats of Benin City, among the largest earthworks built before the mechanical era. By tradition he also introduced bronze-casting through a master craftsman, Iguegha, sent from Ife, the beginning of the art for which the kingdom would become famous. The city-state became an empire under Oba Ewuare the Great (r. c. 1440–1473), who seized the throne after a violent succession struggle, curtailed the power of the uzama over the succession, rebuilt Benin City with a new plan, walls and nine gates, and launched the campaigns that created the first Benin territorial empire. Ewuare is often regarded as Benin's greatest king. His reign divides the earlier city-state from the regional power that reached its greatest extent a century later.
fields.socioeconomy: The Benin economy combined agriculture, craft manufacture of very high quality and long-distance trade linking the West African forest zone to the Atlantic coast and to routes leading north towards the Sahel. The fertile forest lands west of the Niger Delta produced yams, palm oil and kola nuts. Kola was a valuable commodity in Muslim communities across the Sahel, where its mild stimulant properties made it both desirable and religiously permitted. Craft production was organised into hereditary guilds working for the Oba's court: the Igun Eronmwon (brass- and bronze-casters), the Igbesanmwan (ivory and wood carvers), the Owina n'Ido (weavers) and other specialists. Their products were at once religious items, royal regalia, diplomatic gifts and trade goods. Portuguese traders arrived in the 1480s, when João Afonso de Aveiro reached Benin during the reign of Oba Ozolua. Portuguese brass manillas (horseshoe-shaped bracelets used as currency) came into Benin in exchange for pepper, ivory, cloth and captives, and supplied the metal for the great expansion of brass casting that produced the kingdom's most celebrated works. The Oba controlled the main exports, and his court was both the kingdom's leading commercial institution and its centre of artistic production; later Obas, such as Adolo in the nineteenth century, continued to regulate which goods European traders could buy. Britain's abolition of the Atlantic slave trade in 1807, and the subsequent shift to palm-oil commerce dominated by coastal middlemen, eroded the kingdom's trading revenues and contributed to the economic contraction that preceded its final crisis.
fields.military: The Benin army was built on warriors owing personal loyalty to the Oba, supplemented by levies from tributary chiefs. A system of war titles and ranks rewarded martial achievement, with the Iyase and Ezomo as leading war chiefs. Later European accounts credited Benin with the ability to raise as many as 180,000 men. The figure is almost certainly exaggerated, but it reflects the kingdom's capacity for mass mobilisation rather than a standing professional army. The greatest expansion came under Oba Ozolua the Conqueror (c. 1481–1504), who by tradition fought some 200 battles and extended Benin's control in all directions. Oba Esigie (c. 1504–1550) defeated a major Igala invasion from the north around 1515–1516, a victory that secured the north-eastern frontier and inspired much new court ceremony and commemorative art; he also defeated a challenge from his brother Arhuaran at Udo. Oba Orhogbua (c. 1550–1578) is traditionally credited with establishing a garrison at Eko on the island that would become Lagos, extending Benin's influence along a long stretch of the western coast. Like the armies of many pre-colonial African states, Benin's was effective in raids, punitive expeditions and the subjugation of smaller polities, but lacked the logistical base for sustained distant campaigns and had no answer to industrial-era firepower. The British Punitive Expedition of 1897 took and burned Benin City within days, which showed how wide the technological gap had become by the late nineteenth century.
fields.governance: Benin's government was a sacred monarchy. The Oba held great authority, balanced by the palace associations, the hereditary uzama nobles and the town chiefs. He was at once king, chief priest and the living embodiment of the state's continuity: styled Omo n'Oba, he was surrounded by elaborate ritual protocols that governed his daily life and public appearances, and he was believed to possess supernatural powers. Ewuare the Great's reforms in the mid-fifteenth century strengthened royal authority: he reduced the uzama's role in choosing the Oba, promoted succession within the royal line, created the orders of town and palace chiefs that balanced hereditary and royal-appointee interests, and brought the craft guilds under direct royal patronage. The palace complex at Benin City was both the administrative and the religious centre of the kingdom, housing shrines to royal ancestors honoured through the Igue festival and other royal ritual cycles. Provincial government combined appointed chiefs in nearby territories with tributary arrangements in more distant regions, whose rulers acknowledged Benin's overlordship, paid tribute in goods and military service, and sent sons or other dependants to the royal court as pledges of loyalty. The palace pillars were covered with cast brass plaques (conventionally called bronze plaques) depicting royal ceremonies, military victories and court life. They were at once decoration, historical archive and assertion of royal prestige.
fields.impact: The Benin Empire's impact was political, commercial, artistic and, most consequentially, colonial. The kingdom shaped the traditions of government and the identity of the Edo-speaking peoples of southern Nigeria across some seven centuries of dynastic rule. Its institutions survived British conquest, and the Benin monarchy remains a revered traditional institution in Nigeria today. Benin's position between the forest interior and the Atlantic coast made it an important partner in Portuguese, Dutch and British commercial networks from the fifteenth to the nineteenth centuries, and its demand for brass manillas stimulated European metal production on a large scale. The Benin Bronzes are mostly cast brass, produced from the late fifteenth century onward with Portuguese and later Dutch metal, and they form one of the finest bodies of figurative sculpture produced in sub-Saharan Africa. Their arrival in Europe after 1897 challenged prevailing racist assumptions about African artistic capacity and contributed to the growing European appreciation of African art in the early twentieth century. In the 1897 Punitive Expedition several thousand brass, ivory and wooden works were looted and dispersed to museums and private collections worldwide. This has made the Benin Bronzes the central case in the international debate over the restitution of cultural property, and Nigerian and Edo demands for their return from the British Museum, the Ethnological Museum Berlin and many other institutions form one of the most active repatriation processes of the twenty-first century.
fields.decline: Benin declined over nearly three centuries, from the death of the last warrior king Ehengbuda around 1606 to the British Punitive Expedition of 1897. A civil war around 1700 nearly destroyed the kingdom, and the colonial pressures of the nineteenth century hastened the end. The warrior kings who had built the empire, the line of Obas from Ewuare to Ehengbuda who combined military expansion with artistic patronage, ended with Ehengbuda's death. The following century saw shorter, more turbulent reigns in which rival branches of the royal family competed for the throne while the kingdom gradually lost control of outlying territories. The civil war under Oba Ewuakpe (c. 1700–1712) brought Benin closer to collapse than at any time since its founding: the chiefs and people deserted the Oba, the monarchy was nearly abolished, and tradition holds that Ewuakpe was reduced to such poverty that he had to farm his own food. A recovery under Akenzua I and Eresoyen in the first half of the eighteenth century stabilised the kingdom's core, but during the later eighteenth and nineteenth centuries Benin was weakened by violent succession disputes, and weaker Obas withdrew into their palaces and the rituals of divine kingship while granting titles freely. The end of the Atlantic slave trade removed a source of revenue, and the Oba's control of trade became increasingly difficult to maintain against British commercial pressure. The immediate cause of the kingdom's fall was the killing in January 1897 of a British party led by acting Consul-General James Phillips, which had advanced towards Benin City during a sacred festival despite warnings to wait. This provided the pretext for Admiral Harry Rawson's Punitive Expedition, which burned Benin City, looted the palace and exiled Oba Ovonramwen to Calabar, where he died in 1914.
fields.summary: The Benin Empire is best known for the Benin Bronzes, several thousand works in brass, ivory and wood, looted in the British Punitive Expedition of 1897 and dispersed to museums worldwide. They are a supreme artistic achievement of pre-colonial West Africa and the most actively contested artefacts in the debate over cultural restitution, since they show what colonial conquest took and what its descendants are still seeking to recover.
fields.teaser: The Kingdom of Benin in modern Nigeria produced the famous Benin Bronzes, among Africa's greatest artistic achievements. Looted by British forces in 1897, they are now held in museums worldwide, and some have been returned.
fields.t0: An Edo kingdom in southern Nigeria whose Obas built a regional empire from Benin City from the 15th century.
fields.t1: Royal guilds produced the Benin Bronzes, among the finest figurative sculpture of sub-Saharan Africa.
fields.t2: A British expedition burned Benin City in 1897 and looted its art, now at the centre of the restitution debate.
fields.dyk: Much of the metal for the Benin Bronzes came from Portuguese brass manillas, horseshoe-shaped bracelets used as currency in trade.
